strand_a.title: Technological sovereignty in healthcare innovation and production for defence: proposal for an evaluation index to guide European policies
strand_a.authors: Renaud Laffourcade, Ileana Akrichi, Fanny Caputo, P. Cappe de Baillon, Jiska Kentrop, Florence Le Page, Yannick Saintigny
strand_a.source: Global Security: Health, Science and Policy
strand_a.summary: This peer-reviewed article addresses technological sovereignty in healthcare innovation and production for defence purposes. Rather than reporting an empirical measurement exercise, it proposes an evaluation index intended to guide European policy decisions in this area. The paper sets out the dimensions the index covers and argues for its use in assessing where European capability and dependency lie across the innovation and production chain. The work is explicitly European in orientation and sits at the intersection of health research, defence capability and industrial policy. It is a proposal for an instrument; the index is not yet validated through large-scale application, so its results should be read as a framework rather than as measured sovereignty levels.

strand_a.title: Governing knowledge, shaping Europe: research security in the EU’s geopolitical turn
strand_a.summary: The article traces EU and national policy from 2013–2025 across the Netherlands, Germany, Finland, Italy and Hungary. It argues that security rationales are being embedded in ordinary research governance, producing what it calls securitisation through governance and an epistemic form of sovereignty. The design is interpretive comparative process tracing, so the finding concerns institutionalisation and policy translation rather than measured effects on research output.
strand_a.core_message: Research security becomes embedded through multi-level coordination, national translation and routine governance, making scientific openness more conditional.
strand_a.relevance_note: Direct evidence on EU research-security governance, Member State implementation and the changing conditions of international research collaboration.

strand_a.title: The EU’s digital sovereignty and quantum technologies: to what end?
strand_a.authors: Plixavra Vogiatzoglou, Joris V. J. van Hoboken
strand_a.summary: This article examines digital sovereignty as an EU policy objective and argues it is less about what the term suggests than about legitimising points of control. The authors first trace how sovereignty and associated regulation evolved in relation to digital infrastructures, then focus on quantum technologies, which they describe as a recent and comparatively understudied anchor for EU digital sovereignty policy. Their argument is that beneath efforts to assert control and attain independence, digital sovereignty works performatively to construct a European identity, while producing concrete effects: the allocation of funding towards technological goals whose outcomes remain uncertain, and towards a selected set of European actors. The piece is a critical reading of the concept rather than an assessment of whether specific quantum investments succeed.
strand_a.core_message: Digital sovereignty functions primarily to legitimise points of control and to construct European identity performatively, with tangible consequences in directing funds towards uncertain technological goals and select European actors.
strand_a.relevance_note: Offers a sceptical counterweight to the EU's own framing of technological sovereignty, in a technology the EU is actively funding.

strand_a.title: Harmonisation of life cycle assessment practices in horizon Europe battery technology projects
strand_a.authors: Sara M. Pinto, Maria Soares, Emanuel J. Lourenço, Emanuel Glans, Mats Zackrisson, Kristin Fransson, Gemma Mendoza, Guillermo Ormazabal, et al.
strand_a.summary: Life cycle assessment estimates a product's environmental burden across its whole life and is widely used in EU-funded battery research. This paper, from the Battery Heroes sustainability working group, reviews how five Horizon Europe battery projects actually apply it. It finds emerging convergence on several choices: capacity-based functional units of one kilowatt-hour, reliance on ecoinvent databases, and growing adoption of the Environmental Footprint 3.1 method. Substantial variability persists in system boundary definitions, end-of-life and recycling modelling, electricity assumptions and reporting practice, all of which can materially change results. The authors propose a minimum harmonised reporting set to improve comparability and support alignment with the Product Environmental Footprint method and the EU Battery Regulation.

strand_a.title: Self-assessment of research security
strand_a.summary: The Research Council of Finland requires every application to include a research security appendix containing a self-assessment, a description of risk factors and, where necessary, a risk management plan, prepared on a set template. Identifying and assessing research security risks and presenting an adequate management plan at application stage are prerequisites for funding, and insufficient identification or assessment may render an application inadmissible or lead to rejection. The appendix is not peer reviewed but is available to reviewers as part of the application, and for consortia it is submitted by the consortium principal investigator. It can be completed in Finnish, Swedish or English. This is operational funder policy rather than a study or a new announcement.

strand_a.summary: The authors combine the general entrepreneurial-ecosystem framework with elements specific to deep tech, then build a keyword thesaurus to identify deep-tech startups founded between 2019 and 2021. The presence of specialised deep-tech knowledge and talent emerges as the strongest regional predictor, while generic ecosystem quality and specific formal institutions matter less. Findings are cross-sectional associations at regional level, not causal estimates.

strand_a.title: Japan's security policy under Prime Minister Takaichi
strand_a.summary: Sanae Takaichi became Japan's first female prime minister in October 2025 and won a large Diet majority in February 2026. This FIIA briefing argues she is advancing a realism-based security agenda rooted in Shinzo Abe's legacy, now with stronger political backing. Her recorded achievements include expanded defence exports, more dual-use research and development, strengthened intelligence structures and economic-security measures aimed at China. Constitutional revision to recognise Japan's military forces remains her most ambitious and least certain goal. The paper notes heightened tension with China alongside deeper ties with the United States, Australia, the Philippines and Indonesia, and closes by identifying cooperation opportunities for Finland, Europe and NATO as Japan shifts to co-production.

strand_a.title: China and Limits to the European Union's Geoeconomic Turn
strand_a.authors: Alasdair R. Young, Scott A. W. Brown
strand_a.source: JCMS Journal of Common Market Studies
strand_a.summary: The article examines the shift from efficiency to security in EU external economic policy, often called the geoeconomic turn, using China as the test case. It concentrates on two policies at the heart of that rivalry: export controls on advanced semiconductors and restrictions on Chinese fifth-generation telecommunications equipment. Export controls are framed as offensive, aimed at constraining Chinese military and technological capability, while 5G limits are defensive, aimed at protecting critical infrastructure from information extraction or disruption. Both fall under national security and therefore under member state responsibility, which the authors describe as hard cases for EU action. The authors also observe that the EU frames the China challenge around direct risks rather than broad strategic rivalry.
strand_a.core_message: Because export controls and 5G security remain member state competences, they are hard tests of EU geoeconomic power, and the EU frames China primarily as a source of direct risks rather than a broad strategic rival.
strand_a.relevance_note: Central to European technology security, export controls and telecommunications infrastructure policy towards China.

strand_a.reader_more: The article compares Poland, Germany, Spain and Finland using literature, policy documents and secondary European data. It distinguishes the effects associated with Horizon Europe from those associated with structural and regional funding. strand_a.title: Report 'Research careers: A critical choice for Europe'
strand_a.authors: Manuel Heitor, Sophie Ratcliff, Mattias Bjoernmalm, Tanya Bondarouk, Vincent Klein Ikkink (CESAER)
strand_a.summary: This CESAER report, released on 11 December 2024, presents results, insights and recommendations from its 2024 research careers survey. It combines data from 24 universities of science and technology with expert assessment, landscape analysis and detailed case studies. The report finds growth across researcher categories between 2019 and 2024 but stresses that institutional data do not capture the researcher's own perspective, citing evidence that postdoctoral researchers face short-term contracts, job insecurity and mental health strain. It argues the European Commission must lead in creating conditions for research excellence, and it proposes a Choose Europe initiative, calling for it to be launched as a pilot under the Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions. The survey reflects institutional responses from a self-selected association membership.
strand_a.core_message: Research careers in Europe remain unstable enough to drive net talent outflow, and the report proposes a Choose Europe pilot under MSCA as a response.
strand_a.relevance_note: Central European research-policy evidence on research careers, talent retention and brain circulation.

strand_a.title: Rearming Europe for deterrence: Short-term priorities and policy options
strand_a.authors: Centre for European Reform (announcing a policy brief by Armida van Rij)
strand_a.summary: The press release presents Armida van Rij's Centre for European Reform policy brief on short-term European rearmament. It frames the problem as the United States stepping back from European security while Russia intensifies hostile activity. The brief's recommendations fall into three areas: winning public support for rearmament, ensuring equipment and capabilities are actually operational, and building a pipeline of trained personnel. It argues European NATO allies need a realistic assessment of what can fight tonight, and should default to European production where capacity exists, such as ammunition, drones and some air defence, while buying from non-European allies where shortfalls are too large. It also criticises physical entry requirements that screen out people suited to cyber and drone roles.

strand_a.title: EU–LAC Relations in the Context of NATO Geopolitics
strand_a.source: Perspectives on Global Development and Technology
strand_a.summary: EU–LAC Relations in the Context of NATO Geopolitics. Abstract This analysis establishes how NATO geopolitics, operating as the strategic arm of US imperialism, constitutes the primary instrument that conditions relations between the European Union (EU) and Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) in the current global conjuncture. This contradiction manifested itself at the IV EU–CELAC Summit, whose results reflect European subordination to the NATO agenda and its consequent inability to question US military intervention in the Caribbean or to transform the structural mechanisms—such as neocolonial trade agreements—that perpetuate asymmetry, economic reprimarization, and the technological dependence of LAC.

strand_a.reader_what: Argues European subordination to NATO prevented the EU-CELAC summit from addressing structural asymmetries.
strand_a.reader_why: Frames Latin American technological dependence as sustained by trade arrangements the EU will not revisit.
strand_a.reader_more: This article advances an explicitly anti-imperialist reading of relations between the EU and Latin America and the Caribbean. The author's thesis is that NATO geopolitics, characterised as the strategic arm of United States power, is the primary factor conditioning those relations, producing a contradiction with the region's stated interest in autonomous development and its proclamation as a zone of peace. She argues the fourth EU-CELAC summit demonstrated this, reflecting an inability to question United States military intervention in the Caribbean or to change structural mechanisms such as trade agreements that she says perpetuate asymmetry and technological dependence. The conclusion urges the EU to distance itself from NATO. This is a strongly normative polemic rather than a neutral analysis, and its framing is contested.

strand_a.title: European strategic autonomy revisited: Europeanisation, identity and limits to defence integration
strand_a.summary: Russia's war against Ukraine gave European strategic autonomy renewed political momentum, yet the gap between declared ambition and actual defence integration has not closed. This article revisits the concept through Europeanisation theory and questions of European identity, arguing that the limits are not purely material. Member states' differing self-understandings and the uneven way European-level norms are absorbed nationally constrain how far integration can go, regardless of budget commitments. The analysis is conceptual and document-based rather than predictive, and the author is careful to frame persistent ambition-capability gaps as structurally produced rather than temporary.
strand_a.core_message: Europeanisation processes and contested European identity impose structural limits on defence integration that funding commitments alone do not resolve.

strand_a.title: The European Green Deal as transformative innovation policy: principles for transition governance
strand_a.authors: Pieter J. Beers, Amanda Krijgsman, Aniek Hebinck, Chris Foulds, Giorgia Silvestri, Timo Von Wirth
strand_a.summary: The authors treat the European Green Deal, the EU's programme towards climate neutrality by 2050, as transformative innovation policy, noting that its translation into practice has struggled on stakeholder involvement, dominant discourses and policy coordination. Within the SHARED GREEN DEAL project they applied four governance principles across six Green Deal policy domains in workshops involving more than 150 participants, to identify transformative policy pathways towards Green Deal targets. They report that using future imaginaries helped participants understand both the obstacles to and the preconditions for transformation-oriented EU policy, and that identifying pathways together with their trade-offs and co-benefits supports translating EU targets into action. The authors present insights for shaping regional innovation policies across the EU. Findings come from participatory workshops, so they are deliberative outputs rather than measured policy effects.
strand_a.core_message: Applying four governance principles with future imaginaries surfaced obstacles, preconditions and trade-offs for transformation-oriented EU policy across six Green Deal domains.

They report that using future imaginaries helped participants understand both the obstacles to and the preconditions for transformation-oriented EU policy, and that identifying pathways together with their trade-offs and co-benefits supports translating EU targets into action. The authors present insights for shaping regional innovation policies across the EU. Findings come from participatory workshops, so they are deliberative outputs rather than measured policy effects.

strand_a.title: Necessity of AI Sovereignty Initiatives in Finland: A PMT-Based Study of Policy-makers’ Perceptions
strand_a.summary: The thesis asks whether Finland should pursue AI sovereignty initiatives and how policymakers perceive dependence on foreign AI technology. It uses Protection Motivation Theory, which separates perceived severity and vulnerability from beliefs about whether a response would work and whether the actor can carry it out. AI sovereignty is conceptualised across three layers, models, data and infrastructure, and situated within EU regulation and Finland's own constraints: limited domestic compute, competition for specialist talent, and dependence on global supply chains. A structured survey went to all 200 members of the Finnish Parliament and 25 responded. Perceived severity, vulnerability and response efficacy were high while self-efficacy was lower, indicating doubt about independent implementation capacity.
strand_a.core_message: Respondents rated the threat high and responses effective, but expressed lower confidence in Finland's capacity to implement measures independently.

strand_a.summary: This CERRE report offers a three-level framework for mapping AI governance geopolitically. It finds that jurisdictions share broad objectives, including safety, rights, innovation, industrial policy, security and digital sovereignty, but differ in priorities and trade-offs. It distinguishes direct regulatory control from indirect influence over concentrated private power, producing four governance postures. China combines strong state control with subordinated private firms, while United States federal policy has moved toward greater state direction and middle powers favour multilateral harmonisation. strand_a.title: Research Infrastructures as Bottleneck Resources: A Pathway-Based Evaluation of Support in Challenge-Driven Access
strand_a.authors: Nicolas V. Rüffin, Katharina C. Cramer
strand_a.summary: This paper evaluates the first three years of a Horizon Europe project giving researchers transnational access to research infrastructures for circular economy work. It treats such infrastructures as enabling bottleneck resources, whose limited availability, technical complexity and organisational demands can constrain challenge-driven research. Using a multi-method formative evaluation, the authors trace how users progress from first contact through proposal preparation to experiments and early outputs. Dedicated support structures were found to play a central role in lowering barriers, particularly for less experienced applicants, leading the authors to argue for centralised support hubs as a governance mechanism. They also find that academic transnational access mainly supports work at medium technology readiness levels, so different mechanisms are needed for downstream innovation bottlenecks.

strand_a.title: Rethinking dual-use in quantum technology
strand_a.summary: This editorial introduces a ten-paper collection on dual-use quantum technologies. Its central historical claim is that quantum technology was dual-use from the beginning: defence and intelligence agencies funded, shaped and sometimes directly performed the foundational experiments, from the 1954 maser under US naval research support through ion-trapping work at NIST to the 1994 demonstration of entanglement distribution at the UK Defence Research Agency. The authors observe that this history is overwhelmingly American and British, which they offer as part of the explanation for why the link between quantum research and defence is received differently and more recently in continental Europe. They also argue dual-use describes a status rather than settling a moral question.

strand_a.title: SUSTAINABLE AI INTEGRATION IN LOCAL GOVERNANCE: HUMAN RIGHTS, ECONOMIC SUSTAINABILITY AND OVERCOMING DONOR DEPENDENCY
strand_a.authors: Zoia Ivantsova, Vitalii Barvinenko, Natalia Mishyna
strand_a.summary: This article examines AI governance in Ukrainian local self-government, focusing on the interaction between donor dependency, human rights protection and economic sustainability. Using doctrinal, institutional and comparative legal analysis against EU regulatory and policy documents, it argues that donor-supported AI initiatives have delivered short-term benefits for local services and crisis management but remain institutionally fragile once external funding cycles expire. The authors name this a donor dependency trap, characterised by fragmented digital infrastructure, insufficient administrative capacity, weak institutional integration and limited financial sustainability. They also flag human rights concerns around privacy, algorithmic discrimination, transparency of automated decisions and absent appeal mechanisms. Their conclusion is that sustainable integration requires stable domestic financing, transparent procurement, meaningful human oversight and safeguards consistent with the EU AI Act.

strand_a.title: Which job offers may mitigate brain drain? An analysis of Italian PhD students
strand_a.authors: Monique Wangyi Dai, Giulio Marini, Hugo Horta
strand_a.summary: This study uses a discrete choice experiment, in which respondents repeatedly choose between hypothetical job offers, to identify what would keep doctoral students in Italy rather than pushing them abroad. The result runs against the usual expectation. Despite job insecurity, internationally uncompetitive salaries, scarce vacancies and a constrained national labour market, these students, including strong research performers, still prefer to stay. They are reluctant to migrate even when offered non-research jobs lacking autonomy and long-term stability, and salary alone is not the primary determinant of migration decisions. Staying is often experienced as accepting a salary or career penalty in order to continue research in their current country or city.

This study examines the relationship between enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, workforce digital skills, and labour productivity using a quantitative cross-sectional design based on secondary data from Eurostat and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). strand_a.reader_title: Once income is controlled for, AI adoption no longer predicts EU labour productivity
strand_a.reader_what: After controlling for economic development, only GDP per capita significantly predicted labour productivity.
strand_a.reader_why: Indicates digital technology alone does not deliver productivity gains without complementary economic capability.
strand_a.reader_more: This study relates enterprise AI adoption and workforce digital skills to labour productivity across the 27 EU member states, using Eurostat and OECD data in a cross-sectional design. Simple pairwise correlations look encouraging, with productivity positively associated with AI adoption, digital skills and GDP per capita alike. The regression tells a different story: once economic development is controlled for, GDP per capita is the only statistically significant predictor, and the independent effects of AI adoption and digital skills cease to be significant. The authors read this as evidence that digital technologies do not by themselves guarantee productivity gains. Their argument is that complementary economic capabilities are what translate digital transformation into measurable output.

strand_a.title: A sustainable platform for federated health data access, AI innovation, and regulatory acceptance in alignment with the European Health Data Space principles
strand_a.authors: Erwin Boutsma, Katja Herzog, Rebecca C. Rancourt, Torsten Gerriet Blum, Alberto Moreno, Francisco J. Núñez-Benjumea, Hanna Ćwiek-Kupczyńska, Rada Hussein, et al.
strand_a.summary: IDERHA is building one of Europe's first pan-European, disease-agnostic health data spaces, aligned with European Health Data Space principles and designed for compliance with the GDPR and the AI Act. Its technical approach is privacy-by-design: federated analytics and federated learning let analysis run where the data sits, preserving data sovereignty and reducing privacy exposure. strand_a.title: Export controls and the energy transition: Aligning security and sustainability
strand_a.source: Review of European, Comparative & International Environmental Law
strand_a.summary: The article examines how export controls, once driven by narrow security aims, increasingly target advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence and the minerals needed for low-carbon energy. Drawing on the economic statecraft literature, it argues these measures generate unintended consequences for green technology even when not aimed at it: disrupted supply chains, higher compliance burdens, retaliation particularly from China, and the risk of long-term technological bifurcation that slows innovation and raises costs. It makes three contributions: conceptualising the mechanism, comparing US, EU and Chinese strategies, and proposing 'green regionalism' as a framework for aligning export-control cooperation with climate goals. It is doctrinal and conceptual analysis, not empirical measurement.

strand_a.title: A Copernican revolution? Geopolitical tensions, Polish universities and the (dis)continuities of neo-nationalism
strand_a.summary: This article examines how Poland's higher education and research policies were mobilised after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine opened new geopolitical opportunities. Drawing on document analysis and non-local ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2022 and 2023, the author argues the Law and Justice government reframed research policy through securitising discourses of regional leadership and Polish exceptionalism. The study focuses on the creation of the Copernican Academy and activities around Collegium Intermarium, showing how narratives of an Intermarium bloc were instrumentalised to pursue neo-nationalist ambitions in global academic governance. It also documents the reversal: policy changes under the subsequent Tusk-led government have sought to dismantle that institutional legacy.
strand_a.core_message: The Law and Justice government used securitising geopolitical narratives to advance neo-nationalist aims in academic governance through new institutions, appropriating internationalisation discourse to legitimise them; the succeeding government has moved to dismantle this legacy.
strand_a.relevance_note: Shows national research policy being used as an instrument of geopolitical positioning inside the EU.

strand_a.title: General-Purpose AI under the EU AI Act: A Conceptual Allocation of Duties across the Value Chain
strand_a.source: SCRIPTed: A Journal of Law, Technology & Society
strand_a.summary: The article analyses how the adopted EU Artificial Intelligence Act distributes obligations along the AI value chain, focusing on general-purpose or foundation models. It proposes a taxonomy of foundation model providers, fine-tuners, integrators and deployers, and examines the interfaces between them, including model and system documentation and logging. Using principles of control, foreseeability, benefit and capability, it argues that those who design and train foundation models should carry upstream transparency and safety duties, while those adapting or deploying systems carry downstream risk management and oversight. It compares enforcement through market surveillance authorities and the EU AI Office with data protection supervision and flags overlaps needing coordination. It closes with recommendations for standards bodies.

strand_a.title: Opportunities for vein‐to‐vein datasets from a blood establishment perspective: Towards a ‘Pan‐European Transfusion Research InfrAstructure ’
strand_a.authors: Sophie M. T. Wehrens, Mikko Arvas, Suzanne F. Fustolo‐Gunnink, Matea Vinković Vlah, Allison Waters, Christian Erikstrup, Louise Ørnskov Drechsler, Simon J. Stanworth, et al.
strand_a.summary: The Pan-European Transfusion Research Infrastructure project set out first to map which donor and blood establishment databases already exist. An online survey went to European Blood Alliance members and was completed by 17 blood establishments across 16 countries. Most could in principle link donor data to product data, 13 of 17, and to recipient data, 10 of 17, for research purposes, but only 5 had an automated donor-to-recipient linkage. The barriers most often reported were legal constraints and lack of consent, cited by 11 establishments, and resources, cited by between 10 and 14. The authors conclude that early work should focus on helping establishments navigate legal frameworks and on investing in resources and data harmonisation.

strand_a.title: Autonomy through partnerships: Charting the EU's global digital engagement
strand_a.summary: The analysis covers initiatives across all major regions and five domains, showing that EU external digital action now extends well beyond regulation into infrastructure, research, cybersecurity and security cooperation. It describes a shift from a technical, siloed policy area to an instrument of foreign policy, with digital issues embedded in trade agreements and regional dialogues rather than handled separately. The central criticism is that this expansion happened without a fully articulated strategic framework, so the proliferation of instruments has weakened oversight and made the EU's external posture hard to read. Recommendations centre on targeted partnerships for critical technologies, trusted value chains and resilient infrastructure. These are the authors' views, not an EU position.

strand_a.title: The future is fermented: How Europe can succeed in the next industrial race – European Council on Foreign Relations
strand_a.summary: This ECFR report argues that the next industrial transition will be built with microbes as much as machines. Biomanufacturing uses biological processes to produce food, fuels, chemicals and materials that currently depend on fossil resources. The underlying science is long established, but the report contends that advances in artificial intelligence and falling renewable energy costs are turning biomanufacturing from a niche climate technology into a serious industrial proposition. It argues China has grasped this and is moving decisively, while Europe still holds the scientific base to compete but risks losing the window through slow action. The analysis is a strategic argument by a think tank rather than empirical measurement, and its claims about competitive outcomes are projections.

strand_a.title: The EU’s need for a new growth model: Innovation under strategic capitalism
strand_a.summary: Strategic capitalism here describes an environment in which industrial policy, investment screening and export controls have become ordinary instruments of statecraft. The authors argue that Europe's current model, built on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures, is fragile under those conditions, and that its innovation future depends on aligning competitiveness with control over critical economic flows and a clear direction for innovation. They set out four trajectories: Dependent Europe, innovation without control or direction; Fortress Europe, control without dynamism; Fragmented Europe, ambition without alignment; and Strategic Europe, which aligns all three and is the only one they see leading to sustained technological leadership. The scenarios are analytical constructions used to structure the argument rather than predictions.

strand_a.authors: Horia Iuga, Mehmet Ali Balcı, Iulia Cristina Iuga, Ömer Akgüller
strand_a.summary: The study builds country-year indices for health-AI research capacity and equity-adjusted patient value across all 27 EU member states from 2011 to 2024. It estimates two-way fixed-effects models, interactions with out-of-pocket spending, a post-COVID break, threshold tests and multiple robustness checks. strand_a.title: Research security
strand_a.summary: This page sets out the Research Council of Finland's overall position on research security, distinct from its detailed application guidance. The council states it is obliged by law to ensure research security risks are addressed in funded projects, collaborations and the use of results, while the same law specifies that security considerations must not restrict a researcher's choice of topic or methods. It defines research security as anticipating and managing risks in international collaboration, and identifies three categories: transfer of critical knowledge and technology enabling military or intelligence use, harmful interference such as disinformation or induced self-censorship, and uses undermining fundamental rights or European values. Responsibility for the assessment rests with the applicant.
strand_a.core_message: Finnish law requires the national research funder to address research security across funded projects and its own international cooperation, while explicitly barring security considerations from restricting researchers' choice of topic or method.

strand_a.title: ERC Proof of Concept grants: Exploring the innovation potential of ERC-funded research
strand_a.authors: Katarina Henning; Jaime Gomez Ramirez; Susana Nascimento; Line Volkers; Eleni Zika
strand_a.summary: Proof of Concept grants are small follow-on awards, open only to existing ERC grant holders, supporting prototyping, market validation, patenting and stakeholder engagement. Between 2014 and 2023 the scheme funded 1,731 projects across 30 EU and associated countries, an investment of €259 million. Health biotechnology and medical technology account for 43 per cent of the portfolio, followed by advanced materials at 17 per cent, artificial intelligence and information technology at 13 per cent and quantum technologies at 12 per cent. The report is produced by the ERC's own executive agency and reviewed by its innovation working group, so it is self-assessment rather than independent evaluation. The patenting comparison does not adjust for the fact that grantees apply and are selected competitively.
strand_a.core_message: Across 1,731 projects and €259 million between 2014 and 2023, the portfolio is concentrated in health and medical technology, with grantees at least five times more likely to file patents than ERC main-grant-only holders and accounting for nearly half of successful EIC Transition applicants, drawing over €200 million in follow-on funding.

strand_a.title: Shared gains, secure links: rethinking EU-Asia digital cooperation – CEPS
strand_a.summary: The report assesses partnerships pursued under the EU's 2025 International Digital Strategy with Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, 6G and cybersecurity. Its diagnosis is institutional: many actors with overlapping but misaligned interests, spanning EU bodies, member states, partner ministries, industry and civil society, plus wide variation in depth, from South Korea's full Digital Partnership and Horizon Europe association status to Taiwan's informal channels. Being like-minded, the authors argue, does not guarantee aligned interests, and the stated move from a hub-and-spoke model to a network approach remains aspirational. They recommend widening engagement to smaller firms, start-ups, labour organisations and civil society, and building sectoral groupings among smaller sets of partners.
strand_a.core_message: EU-Asia digital partnerships operate in a fragmented ecosystem without unifying institutional or legal architecture, so goals remain underachieved; the authors recommend anchoring alignment in research and innovation collaboration, broadening engagement beyond governments, and using sectoral minilateral formats, with non-recognition-dependent channels for Taiwan.

strand_a.authors: Flavia Lucenti, Céleste Bonnamy, Thomas Christiansen, Ville Sinkkonen, Sophie Vanhoonacker
strand_a.summary: ABSTRACT This article examines the EU's evolving narratives concerning the governance of digital technologies, focusing on the intersection of geopolitical challenges and internal policymaking through the lens of the strategic narratives approach. strand_a.reader_more: This study models drivers of energy-related carbon emissions across the 27 EU member states from 1996 to 2023, using an extended STIRPAT framework estimated with ridge regression. Unusually, it brings geopolitical risk and energy transition into the model alongside the more familiar economic and technological factors. GDP and unemployment are both significantly positively associated with emissions, while research and development spending is significantly negatively associated. The authors then project four futures: a baseline, policy-driven decarbonisation, market-driven decarbonisation, and a comprehensive low-carbon transition. strand_a.title: Sustainable productivity growth in agriculture: The role of shifts in R&D investments and technology
strand_a.authors: Zuzana Smeets Křístková; Michiel van Dijk; Robert M'Barek; Hans van Meijl; Tomas Ratinger
strand_a.summary: This study evaluates long-term prospects for sustainable agricultural productivity growth under different assumptions about public agricultural research spending, treating that spending as the key productivity driver. It also asks what happens if research focus shifts from maximising yield towards technologies that save inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides. Using the MAGNET computable general equilibrium model, the projections identify China, India and Brazil as regions gaining high productivity growth from agricultural research, while Sub-Saharan Africa struggles with low growth and substantially rising greenhouse gas emissions. Overall emissions are projected to grow faster than agricultural output. The authors find sustainable growth becomes feasible if high-income countries reorient research programmes, with chemical input use falling by as much as 30 percent and limited effect on food prices.

strand_a.summary: The study exploits the sharp scoring cut-off used to award the Small and Medium Enterprise Instrument, the first European research and development subsidy aimed at small firms. strand_a.title: Path dependence and network effects of the GDPR
strand_a.summary: The article explains the global influence of the General Data Protection Regulation through two mechanisms. Path dependence accounts for how earlier European data-protection choices shaped the present regime and constrain its future. Network effects account for why the regime keeps growing: the more jurisdictions and firms operate inside it, the more valuable membership becomes, which holds existing members in and attracts newcomers. Together these make the EU's leading position self-reinforcing rather than merely coercive, and the authors read the Commission's proposed Digital Omnibus as pointing the same way. The analysis is theoretical and interpretive, and does not quantify adoption or the strength of the claimed effects.
strand_a.core_message: GDPR's global position is sustained by path dependence in its origins and by network effects that make continued membership of the regime increasingly attractive.

strand_a.title: Expanding the scope and scale of the EU’s DLT market infrastructures
strand_a.summary: The article traces EU regulation of distributed ledger technology in financial markets from Regulation (EU) 2022/858 to the proposed Market Integration and Supervision Package. It sets out the value proposition of tokenisation, namely atomic settlement and fractionalisation, and contrasts successes such as Project Guardian with failures such as the Australian exchange's CHESS replacement. The authors identify a ceiling on success built into the pilot regime: restrictive capitalisation thresholds and no native cash leg. They assess ESMA's 2025 recommendations and the Commission's response, which would unbundle central securities depository services into DLT notaries and account keepers and raise aggregate thresholds to one hundred billion euros. They conclude that success depends on European technological sovereignty and agile national supervision rather than premature centralisation.
strand_a.core_message: The DLT Pilot Regime's restrictive thresholds and missing cash leg capped adoption; the proposed MISP would create a permanent, far larger architecture whose success hinges on European technological sovereignty.

strand_a.title: Smart Innovations and Sustainability in EU Waste Material Trading: Evidence of Quantile Decomposition in EU Circular Economy Transitions
strand_a.authors: Eszter Lukacs, Peter Nemeth, Md. Rashed, Mohammad Fakhrul Islam
strand_a.summary: The study uses fourteen years of cross-border waste recovery data, 2010 to 2023, across all 27 EU countries. It applies method of moments quantile regression to separate median and dispersion effects, with bootstrap quantile regression for robustness, generalised method of moments for persistence and endogeneity, and Granger causality tests for direction. R&D intensity shows robust positive associations across all quantiles with forward Granger causality, while AI innovation shows no significant association, which the authors read as a possible deployment gap. Municipal waste recycling rates rise monotonically across quantiles with bidirectional causality. These are associations from observational panel data, so causal claims remain limited.

strand_a.title: Bayesian dynamic analysis on innovation adjustment to SME human capital capacity in EU regions
strand_a.authors: Emmanuel Mamatzakis, Christos Staikouras, Constantinos Tsamadias
strand_a.summary: The paper examines how the human capital capacity of small and medium enterprises shapes regional innovation performance across EU NUTS2 regions from 2018 to 2025. They estimate a dynamic Bayesian panel model with a lagged dependent variable. Results show strong path dependence in regional innovation and support a threshold reading: above a critical level of small firm human capital, business research and development has larger short and long run effects, while below it the effect is not statistically significant.

strand_a.reader_what: Case study across seven regions finds limited commercialisation stems from functional misalignment, not resource scarcity.
strand_a.reader_why: Implies adding more support instruments will not help without integrating the governance behind them.
strand_a.reader_more: This paper addresses why Europe produces strong science but comparatively few ventures from public research, interpreting the gap as a knowledge filter problem arising from misalignment between innovation systems and entrepreneurial ecosystems. The authors define alignment as a multi-dimensional governance condition spanning structural, functional and resource domains, and position regional public actors as orchestrators of it. Empirically they study academic spin-offs across seven European regions, identifying recurrent systemic tensions and governance archetypes. Their central result is that limited commercialisation stems less from structural constraints or resource scarcity and more from functional misalignments. The policy implication they draw is pointed: improving commercialisation requires better functional integration of governance structures and resource systems, not simply more support instruments.

strand_a.title: Green patenting within R&D host regions: technology sourcing and reverse spillover effects
strand_a.summary: The sample covers 231 leading corporate research spenders with inventive activity spread across 118 European regions between 2000 and 2018. Using fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models, with a control function approach to address reverse causation, the authors find that higher green innovation intensity in a host region is associated with both whether and how many green patents the local research unit files. The association holds only under specific conditions: the host region is foreign to the firm, lies in Europe's core, is environmentally polluting, and regulates more strictly than the firm's home country. Knowledge in the region itself, rather than activity in neighbouring regions, drives the pattern. Patents measure inventive output imperfectly and the data end in 2018.
strand_a.core_message: Host-region green innovation intensity is significantly associated with both the occurrence and the count of green patents from resident corporate R&D units, indicating reverse technological spillovers from local context into corporate research, but only where the region is foreign, core, environmentally brown and more strictly regulated than the firm's home country.
strand_a.relevance_note: Bears on whether attracting corporate R&D into European regions builds local green technological capability, a live question for regional and industrial policy.

strand_a.title: Does Entrepreneurial Churn Reach Incumbent R&D? Corruption, Time Horizons, and Evidence from Large European Firms
strand_a.summary: The study merges Orbis firm data with Eurostat indicators for 1,693 large firms in 19 European countries during 2017–2023. Fixed-effects models find no robust within-firm relationship between business registrations or bankruptcies and R&D intensity. Institutional conditions, especially corruption, show more persistent relationships and different short- versus long-run patterns. Administrative churn measures are imperfect proxies for entrepreneurial dynamics, which the authors treat as a key limitation.
strand_a.core_message: Aggregate entrepreneurial churn does not robustly explain within-firm R&D intensity; institutional conditions carry more signal.

strand_a.title: Rethinking technological complexity and investment: a sectoral analysis in the EU 1995–2020
strand_a.summary: The authors build an index of technological complexity for each economic sector, then use econometric methods to relate sectoral investment to complexity, consumption, interest rates and foreign direct investment across EU countries from 1995 to 2020. Their reading is that divergence inside the Union is structural: an export-led growth model in the north and a credit-supported consumption model in the south left peripheral economies investing in less complex activities, which the authors connect to the break-up of industrial sectors in weaker member states. The complexity index is their own construction, so the results depend on how it is built. The analysis establishes patterns and associations across countries and sectors rather than proving a single cause of divergence.
strand_a.core_message: The sectoral composition of peripheral EU economies did not shift toward more technologically complex activities over 1995-2020, which the authors link to industrial disintegration in weaker economies and to the need for a redesigned industrial policy.
strand_a.relevance_note: Provides long-run evidence on intra-EU technological divergence directly relevant to European industrial and cohesion policy design.

It uses a structured documentary review and gap analysis across the United States, European Union, United Kingdom, Japan and Singapore. The central finding is a mismatch from both directions: the telecom standards stack is mature on architecture and baseline security but weak on explainability, post-deployment AI assurance, model provenance and human-override regimes, while horizontal AI laws lack telecom-specific operational depth. strand_a.title: Emerging and established topics in drone research: Citation impact and knowledge flows across China, the United States, the EU, Ukraine, and Russia (2020-2025)
strand_a.authors: Myroslava Hladchenko (Centre for R&D Monitoring (ECOOM), University of Antwerp)
strand_a.summary: This preprint analyses emerging and established topics in drone research across China, the United States, the EU, Ukraine and Russia between 2020 and 2025, using OpenAlex bibliographic data. It finds growing geopolitical asymmetries in scientific production, citation concentration and international knowledge exchange, with China increasingly dominating output, fractional authorship contribution and domestic citation circulation while United States and EU publications retain more internationally distributed citation structures. At the same time, China-affiliated publications became more integrated into global citation networks, particularly through exchange with the US and European countries. The author notes that a high proportion of publications with unidentified affiliations complicates interpretation of authorship and citation patterns. This is a preprint and has not been through journal peer review.

strand_a.title: Germany’s AI Divide
strand_a.summary: This data brief maps Germany's AI workforce of roughly 117,000 people, about double Italy's, across sixteen states and many industries. It finds a tension between scale and concentration: Berlin has the densest AI workforce relative to population, while Bavaria and Baden-Wurttemberg hold the largest absolute numbers. Internationally trained professionals tend to enter through startups in cities like Berlin and Hamburg rather than the southern industrial firms, so policies to attract foreign researchers are distinct from building pipelines into legacy industry. Talent broadly tracks the federal AI strategy's priority sectors, with strong representation in manufacturing and robotics, but healthcare is a marked exception at roughly 3,500 professionals, about three percent of the total.
strand_a.core_message: Germany's AI workforce is large but unevenly organised, with retention of domestic graduates, recruitment from abroad and distribution across priority sectors constituting three distinct problems; healthcare in particular is badly under-supplied despite being a stated national priority.
strand_a.relevance_note: Maps the human capital base underlying European AI capability in the EU's largest economy.

strand_a.title: Scientific collaboration, research funding, and novelty in scientific knowledge
strand_a.authors: Hyunha Shin, Keungoui Kim, Dieter F. Kogler
strand_a.summary: The authors use Web of Science publications from European regions between 2008 and 2017, measuring collaboration at five levels from country down to institution and measuring novelty from keyword combinations. They find a significant negative relationship between scientific collaboration and novelty. Funded papers also show lower novelty than unfunded ones, though funding significantly moderates the collaboration-novelty relationship. The authors frame this as extending bibliometric work by linking collaboration levels and funding sources to article novelty. The results are associations in bibliometric data, and the keyword-based novelty indicator is one operationalisation among several possible ones.

strand_a.title: The Neo-Academic Cold War: Political Traumas and Transnational Paranoia
strand_a.summary: This paper argues that an emerging new cold war has produced a neo-academic cold war, structurally different from the last one. Where the previous era featured bipolar US-Soviet competition with separate scientific ecosystems, the author describes today's as multipolar, with semi-autonomous silos of transnational science cooperation and science diplomacy. He traces this to a sequence of global shocks: the September 2001 attacks, war and economic displacement, the rise of neonationalism and illiberal democracies, Russia and China re-emerging as adversaries to the US and EU, Brexit, the pandemic, and the second Trump presidency. He identifies China and Europe as beneficiaries of declining American scientific capability and protectionism, and open science and global problem-solving capacity as the losers.
strand_a.core_message: Global science is fragmenting into semi-autonomous cooperation silos under multipolar rivalry, with China and Europe positioned as relative beneficiaries of US decline and open science and collective problem-solving as the principal casualties.
strand_a.relevance_note: Directly examines fragmentation of global science and argues Europe may gain relative room as US scientific openness and capability weaken.

strand_a.title: Strategic autonomy and Europe's new logic of intervention
strand_a.summary: The brief argues that the war in Ukraine and renewed transatlantic uncertainty are changing what European intervention means. Where the EU once exported crisis management and statebuilding, it now increasingly finances arms production and embeds itself in a wartime economy. The authors observe that combined EU defence budgets have risen by more than half in real terms, and that strategic autonomy is materialising concretely as defence-industrial coordination, direct financing of arms production and military training at unprecedented scale. They also argue that EU engagement with Ukraine blurs the established distinction between donor and recipient, embedding European defence production in a new way. This is an interpretive policy analysis rather than a quantitative evaluation of outcomes.

strand_a.title: The anchor trap and the absorptive capacity: Divergent paths of university-induced economic growth in core and peripheral European regions by PLS-SEM analysis
strand_a.authors: Orsolya Gregán, Sándor Kovács, Zoltán Gabnai
strand_a.source: Journal of Open Innovation Technology Market and Complexity
strand_a.summary: The anchor trap and the absorptive capacity: Divergent paths of university-induced economic growth in core and peripheral European regions by PLS-SEM analysis. As universities transition beyond their traditional Third Mission, they increasingly participate in complex, Quintuple and N-tuple helix open innovation ecosystems, balancing technology commercialization with pressing sustainability demands. Utilizing Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), the empirical results demonstrate that while regional scientific and human capital exhibits a strong positive association with regional GDP and employment, a direct conversion of technological innovation outputs into economic growth is absent at the aggregate level, potentially pointing to a “Regional Innovation Paradox”.

strand_a.reader_title: University research raises regional prosperity mainly in dense metropolitan hubs
strand_a.reader_what: Returns to academic excellence concentrate in metropolitan hubs; peripheral universities instead stabilise local economies.
strand_a.reader_why: Peripheral universities act as anchor institutions, a role that patent and spin-off counts miss.
strand_a.reader_more: This study examines 301 universities across the European Economic Area, relating innovation outputs such as Horizon 2020 participation, patents and spin-offs, together with sustainability profiles, to regional economic and labour market outcomes. Regional scientific and human capital is strongly associated with regional GDP and employment, but technological innovation outputs show no direct conversion into growth at aggregate level, which the authors call a regional innovation paradox. Environmental sustainability performance is positively linked to innovation capacity, while social sustainability outcomes appear structurally decoupled in the short run. A multi-group analysis reveals the spatial asymmetry behind the aggregate result: returns concentrate in high-density metropolitan hubs with strong absorptive capacity, whereas in low-density peripheral regions universities function primarily as anchor institutions stabilising local economies.

deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Partial least squares structural equation modelling on 301 European Economic Area universities, with multi-group analysis comparing metropolitan and peripheral regions.
deep_analysis.qualification: Cross-sectional associations rather than causal estimates; the absence of an aggregate effect does not establish that innovation outputs have none, and the anchor institution role is inferred from group differences.

strand_a.title: The role of the non-academic staff heterogeneity in the performance of European universities
strand_a.authors: Alessandro Avenali, Cinzia Daraio, Simone Di Leo, Joanna Wolszczak-Derlacz
strand_a.summary: The authors examine whether expanding administrative and technical staff helps or hinders European universities. They treat the heterogeneity of non-academic staff as an unobserved factor and estimate it nonparametrically, then test its effect on performance across a sample of 401 European universities. The share of non-academic staff turns out to have no statistically significant effect on efficiency. The latent heterogeneity factor, capturing qualitative and structural differences beyond size and composition, does significantly shape both the efficient frontier and the spread of inefficiency. The result is associational and rests on the chosen frontier specification rather than on any experimental design.
strand_a.core_message: The proportion of non-academic staff does not significantly affect efficiency, but their unobserved heterogeneity significantly influences both the frontier and the distribution of inefficiencies.

strand_a.title: Joint statement: Call for widely spread Horizon Europe call deadlines respecting ERA engagements towards research managers
strand_a.summary: CESAER and The Guild member universities jointly called on the European Commission and Member States to ensure widely spread and predictable call deadlines under the research and innovation framework programmes. The statement notes that 2025 Horizon Europe deadlines clustered in September because the work programme was finalised late and policy priorities shifted, placing undue strain on research managers. It argues that good proposals depend on sustained collaboration between researchers and skilled research managers, which requires a manageable workload across the year, and that compressed timelines force research support offices to scale back services. It warns that a single deadline for most proposals risks privileging institutions with large support offices over smaller ones, cutting against the excellence principle. It asks for piloted adjustments to deadline timing.

strand_a.title: When less data is better: Exploratory privacy-by-design in AI-based human resource analytics based on synthetic data
strand_a.authors: Cristina Iancu, Simona‐Vasilica Oprea, Adela Bârã, Denisa-Maria Iordache
strand_a.source: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences
strand_a.summary: This proof-of-concept study tests whether removing personal identifiers from human resources data changes how large language models evaluate employees, using self-hosted open models as a security layer and a synthetic dataset. Two experiments covered automated redaction of identifying information and the effect of pseudonymisation on model-generated promotion suitability scores. Removing protected attributes preserved overall consistency of scores while reducing identity-linked variation. Most evaluations, 88 percent, were unaffected by identifier visibility, but 12 percent shifted, and Bayesian modelling identified geographic region as the strongest factor linked to that variation, with some non-European profiles scoring lower in certain conditions. The authors stress these are exploratory results needing validation on real data.

strand_a.title: A 'normal' research trap limits scientific breakthroughs and disruptive innovation in the European Union

strand_a.title: Signals of Change, Summer 2026
strand_a.summary: Business Finland Foresight compiled its monthly signals from March to May 2026 into four reinforcing development paths. These are a systemic techno-geoeconomic bifurcation driven by US-China export controls and competing AI ecosystems; a deepening securitisation of markets and industrial policy, including the EU's move toward enforceable exclusion of high-risk vendors; alliance-based industrialisation that embeds defence, technology and supply chains into tightly coupled blocs; and the scaling of China's state-driven self-reliance model. The report draws out grey zones where allies align in principle but diverge on cost-sharing and sovereignty. It is a signal-scanning exercise, so its paths are interpretive rather than forecast.
strand_a.core_message: Economic, technological and defence policy are converging into a single strategic domain in which security criteria increasingly determine market access.

strand_a.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Research: Individual Benefits, Collective Risks, and a Framework for Responsible Research with AI
strand_a.authors: Fulvio Castellacci, Tommaso Ciarli, Yuan Gao, Marianna Marino, Giacomo Marzi, Massimo Riccaboni, María Savona, Simone Vannuccini
strand_a.summary: We propose Responsible Research with AI (RRAI), an extension of the Responsible Research and Innovation tradition organized around four principles that operate at different levels of the research system: disclosure, differentiation, narrative, and proportionality. We argue that the divergence between private and social returns arises through three analytically distinct mechanisms, namely information asymmetry, negative externalities on a shared knowledge base, and depletion of research capacity, and that each calls for a different governance instrument. RRAI builds on existing institutional scaffolding, including the EU AI Act, UNESCO, and the OECD, and aims to preserve AI's productivity gains while addressing systemic risks that individual researchers can neither observe nor manage on their own.
strand_a.core_message: The empirical case for AI's productivity, augmentation, and democratization effects has strengthened.

strand_a.title: Making Public Compute Work for Applied AI Startups
strand_a.summary: The evidence is ten semi-structured interviews in Poland, the fourth-largest national recipient of EU AI factory funding: one AI factory host, four industry and research intermediaries, and five startups in regulated or strategic sectors such as health, life sciences, space and defence. The authors reframe the usual argument about whether public compute is justified, asking instead for whom and on what terms it works. Free access to high-performance computing is welcomed provided it is quick to obtain, protects data and intellectual property, comes with local human support, and allows switching between public facilities and commercial cloud. Gigafactories are seen as extra capacity rather than a different offer. Ten interviews in one country is a narrow base, so these are indicative requirements.

strand_a.reader_what: Review of 59 European energy models finds material demand exceeds Europe proportional share of reserves for seven materials.
strand_a.reader_why: Shows climate scenarios may be materially infeasible without efficiency, recycling and demand reduction.
strand_a.reader_more: The study notes that most energy system models ignore how much material their scenarios would consume, leaving the physical feasibility of decarbonisation pathways untested. The authors combine a systematic review of 59 highly decarbonised European energy system modelling studies with an after-the-fact quantitative assessment of material demand for five key technologies and nineteen materials. Demand exceeds Europe population-based share of current global reserves for seven materials, most clearly gallium, indium, iridium and tellurium and less sharply silver, selenium and vanadium, particularly when several energy sectors are modelled together. Competing non-energy demand worsens the gap. The authors conclude that efficiency, recycling, reserve expansion and innovation can only partly close it and call for sufficiency measures.

strand_a.reader_title: Cohesion Policy transfers show no robust effect on development traps, but research spending does
strand_a.reader_what: Transfers did not robustly reduce regional entrapment risk, while higher research spending consistently did.
strand_a.reader_why: Suggests current allocation may underserve the low research-intensity regions most at risk.
strand_a.reader_more: This paper tests whether European Cohesion Policy fiscal transfers reduce the risk that EU regions fall into a development trap, meaning prolonged stagnation relative to peers. It uses a regression discontinuity design with heterogeneous treatment effects over 2000 to 2020, exploiting eligibility thresholds to approximate a causal comparison. The results do not robustly confirm a direct role for the transfers in reducing entrapment risk. Regions with higher research and development spending, however, consistently show reduced risk, which the author reads as evidence that such spending sustains long-term productivity and growth. The conclusion drawn is that the current fund allocation strategy may inadequately support regions with low research intensity and should be reassessed.

deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Regression discontinuity design with heterogeneous treatment effects on EU regional data, 2000 to 2020.
deep_analysis.qualification: A null result on the direct transfer effect is not proof of no effect; the R&D result is an association within the same design, not an established causal channel. Based on the abstract.

strand_a.title: Policy Brief 2/2026 Promoting Green Lead Market Formation
strand_a.authors: Matti Pihlajamaa, Ville Valovirta, Helmi Hamalainen, Pauli Komonen
strand_a.summary: The brief argues Finland's difficulty is not weak research and development but weak translation of it into scalable business, with R&D investment and high-tech exports having fallen behind peer countries over a decade. Public R&D investment is rising, but many innovations remain stuck in the valley of death because commercialisation and scaling stall. The prevailing policy response, export and internationalisation support, works when global markets already exist, but not when an innovation requires customers to change purchasing and use practices. The authors introduce lead markets, regions that pioneer adoption and shape global diffusion, as a rationale for innovation policy, focus on green lead markets, and argue cross-border Nordic collaboration matters for small open economies. It proposes instruments rather than evaluating them.

strand_a.authors: Teddy Ferdinan, Bartłomiej Koptyra, Mikołaj Langner, Tomasz Adamczyk, Łukasz Radliński, Maciej Markiewicz, Aleksander Szczęsny, Stanisław Woźniak, et al.
strand_a.summary: In this survey, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of RLM adoption across 28 scientific disciplines following the classification used by the European Research Council (ERC), spanning the Social Sciences and Humanities, Physical Sciences and Engineering, and Life Sciences. Reasoning4Sciences: Bridging Reasoning Language Models to All Scientific Branches. While Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) are rapidly emerging as powerful tools for scientific research, their impact is primarily concentrated in "hard science" fields.

strand_a.reader_title: Reasoning AI models adopted unevenly across scientific disciplines
strand_a.reader_what: Survey across 28 research fields finds reasoning language model adoption concentrated in hard sciences, widening productivity gaps.
strand_a.reader_more: The paper surveys adoption of reasoning language models, meaning AI systems designed for multi-step inference, across 28 scientific disciplines using the European Research Council classification covering social sciences and humanities, physical sciences and engineering, and life sciences. The authors argue that impact is concentrated in hard science fields and that slow adoption elsewhere is widening a gap in research productivity. They examine how these models are developed, evaluated and applied by discipline, and introduce a maturity assessment framework based on the domain-specific development and evaluation resources available. Disparities in maturity are substantial and become more pronounced when only publicly available resources are counted. The paper closes with implementation patterns, challenges and directions for broader adoption.

strand_a.title: Selective Conditionality: The EU’s Emerging Approach to Foreign Investment
strand_a.summary: The paper argues the Industrial Accelerator Act introduces selective conditionality into EU foreign direct investment policy, attaching requirements on local employment, supplier integration, R&D, ownership and technology transfer to investment in strategic sectors. The authors see this as narrowly targeted rather than broadly protectionist, affecting mainly large Chinese investments in electric vehicles and batteries. Evidence from the battery sector shows foreign investment closed supply gaps but produced only modest technological spillovers for European firms. They judge the mechanism unlikely to exert much leverage as designed, and call for tighter enforceable conditions, targeted trade policy and a coherent industrial policy. The assessment is prospective.

strand_a.title: Building Resilient and Robust Clean Energy Supply Chains: Challenges and Opportunities for a Sustainable Energy Transition
strand_a.summary: The report synthesises a workshop co-organised by the Commission's Joint Research Centre and the IEA Expert Group on R&D Priority Setting and Evaluation, held at Petten on 27-28 November 2025. Discussion covered geopolitical pressures on supply chains, strategies for data collection and sharing, and modelling techniques for supply-chain mapping. The central consensus was that granular, high-quality data is a precondition for evidence-based policy, against obstacles of fragmentation, commercial opacity and component complexity. Proposed monitoring methods included AI harvesting of unstructured corporate data, satellite imagery of facility construction, and certificate-based component origin mapping. It reports proceedings and expert consensus rather than new empirical results.

strand_a.title: Malta: Microbiome insights to boost healthy ageing
strand_a.summary: This is a funder case study of DPHAGE, a Eureka project between the Maltese company The BioArte and United Kingdom-based TopMD. The project built a diagnostic platform using full-length 16S ribosomal RNA microbiome sequencing to identify biomarkers linked to dementia and irritable bowel syndrome, with the aim of supporting individually tailored treatment plans. The account is written by the funding network and reports project milestones rather than independently assessed clinical performance.

strand_a.title: A world of data in a few hands
strand_a.summary: Simone Turchetti writes from the ERC-funded NEWORLDatA project, which examines how the diplomacy of research data has shaped global science over the past century. He sets the work against the European Framework for Science Diplomacy, an 89-page report that treats data sharing and openness as pillars of international research cooperation. His argument is that data governance has historically favoured a few powerful actors rather than operating as a neutral universal resource, so openness alone will not deliver equitable global science. This is a researcher's interpretive essay drawing on project findings, not a peer-reviewed presentation of results.

strand_a.title: How to Operationalise a Transatlantic Cyber Policy Research Initiative (TCPRI)
strand_a.summary: The EU and US agreed in 2016 to create a Transatlantic Cyber Policy Research Initiative, but three years later the commitment remained largely on paper. This paper takes up the idea and works out how it could actually be run: who convenes it, how researchers and policymakers connect, and what working methods suit a fast-changing threat landscape. strand_b.title: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation
strand_b.authors: Musarat Kabir-Chisty
strand_b.summary: The paper argues that prevailing AI governance frameworks, built on ethics, transparency, risk management and compliance, assume the human processes and expertise being embedded into AI systems have already been captured accurately. It reframes AI adoption as a technology-transfer problem, borrowing from pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, aerospace and advanced manufacturing, where success depends on reproducibility and validation, traceability and knowledge preservation, and process control with continuous verification. To operationalise this it introduces the AI Technology Transfer Framework, a seven-stage governance model for moving workflows, expertise and decision-making into AI systems while retaining accountability and organisational memory. It is a conceptual framework from an integrative review, not an empirically tested method.
strand_b.core_message: AI adoption is better understood as technology transfer, and the seven-stage AI Technology Transfer Framework operationalises that view for organisational governance.
strand_b.relevance_note: Potentially a transferable governance framework for AI adoption, but the substance behind the seven stages is unverified.
strand_b.metadata_note: Crossref omitted the abstract; text was recovered from DOI publisher metadata before the ordinary admission gate.

strand_b.summary: The report was produced for the UK National Federated Compute Services Flexible Fund, combining stakeholder interviews, a demand-side survey, a literature review and a simulation study to examine how federated research computing is actually allocated. strand_b.summary: The paper addresses two kinds of fragmentation in smart city research: conceptual disagreement about what a smart city is, and heterogeneity in how smart city architectures are actually built. From this it derives an integrative definition conceptualising the smart city as a learning, cyber-socio-technical urban system integrating digital infrastructures and data resources. strand_b.title: Country-level innovation performance: introducing sustainable innovation efficiency
strand_b.authors: Yong Tan, Yu Zhao
strand_b.summary: The authors argue that measuring innovation efficiency alone gives an incomplete picture of national innovation performance, and introduce sustainable innovation efficiency to capture how well a country converts research and development inputs into stable outputs when those inputs fluctuate. Using Data Envelopment Analysis on thirty countries from 2009 to 2018, they find overall innovation efficiency is low, with scores consistently below 0.25. High-income countries score better on sustainable innovation efficiency, while lower-middle-income countries score highest on plain innovation efficiency. East Asia and the Pacific outperform Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East and North Africa on innovation efficiency, with variation on the sustainable measure. The construct is new, so its external validity is not yet established.

strand_b.summary: This paper responds to the absence of common experimental standards in deep learning, particularly in natural language processing, compared with more established disciplines. strand_b.summary: TechIntel-MAS is an eight-role multi-agent system built on the CrewAI framework that converts disclosed patent filings and a free-text intelligence request into a structured competitive-intelligence report. Six frontier models run the generative roles in parallel while a separate evaluator pool operates verifier, telemetry and judge roles, so no model evaluates its own output. strand_b.authors: Xinyu Jiang, Ian Belton, George Wright
strand_b.summary: A 2025 paper argued that expert judgments in large science and technology Delphi surveys are systematically biased. This article disputes that. It argues the original authors misread what Delphi is for, conflated disagreement with bias, and analysed secondary data without sufficient rigour. In place of that diagnosis it proposes a cleaner design: distinguish legitimate differences of opinion between experts and non-experts from genuine cognitive or motivational bias, and treat the reasons panelists write for their answers as the primary material for both practice and controlled study. The contribution is a research design, not new survey results.

strand_b.title: Macrohistorical Cycle Synchronization as a Method for Long‐Range Foresight: The Ten Mega Epochs Model
strand_b.authors: Tuomo Kuosa
strand_b.summary: Most foresight looks a decade or two ahead. This article proposes a method for looking much further. It synthesises five nested cycles — from decadal innovation waves up to century-long institutional rhythms — and argues that they periodically fall into step, producing what the author calls a Mega Epoch about every 250 years. The method is demonstrated by mapping 2,500 years of Western history into ten such epochs, drawing on macrohistorians including Ibn Khaldun, Toynbee, Kondratieff, Strauss and Howe, and Turchin. The author states the framework is non-deterministic, open to falsification, and dependent on assumptions such as stable generation length.

strand_b.summary: Financial systems under heavy institutional and geopolitical constraint are hard to forecast with conventional tools. This study builds a foresight framework around the Futures Triangle, which sets future-oriented goals against present pressures and inherited institutional limits. It adds a fuzzy multi-criteria step that scores candidate drivers on importance, uncertainty and rate of change, making the reduction from a long driver list to a working set explicit rather than tacit. Sixty drivers were drawn from expert interviews, regulatory papers and international foresight reports, producing three configurations for Iran's banking sector. The framework is the transferable part; the Iranian application is the demonstration.
strand_b.core_message: Three configurations emerge — structural inertia, managed transition and transformational leap — distinguished by technological capacity, regulatory flexibility and institutional readiness.
strand_b.relevance_note: Strand B is geography-independent; the transferable element is the combination of Futures Triangle structuring with transparent fuzzy driver prioritisation.

strand_b.title: A comparison of two methods for expert elicitation in health technology assessments
strand_b.authors: Bogdan Grigore, Jaime Peters, Christopher Hyde, Ken Stein
strand_b.summary: When data needed for decision-model parameters are missing, formal elicitation of expert judgement can characterise the uncertainty. The authors asked clinical experts to express judgements as probability distributions using two methods, the histogram and the hybrid approach, presented in random order, within a prostate cancer cost-effectiveness model. Distributions were aggregated with and without weighting and fed into probabilistic analysis, and using expert opinion cut the expected value of perfect information at the thirty thousand pound per QALY threshold by 74 to 86 percent. Experts found the histogram method easier but felt the hybrid method captured their views more accurately. Only six of twenty-seven invited experts completed the task, which limits the comparison.
strand_b.core_message: The two elicitation methods produced broadly similar decision conclusions, while including expert opinion markedly reduced decision uncertainty.
strand_b.relevance_note: A transferable evaluation design for expert elicitation, relevant wherever expert judgement feeds quantitative assessment.
